questions.reason: Chat Completions `stream` description: 'partial message deltas will be sent ... Tokens will be sent as data-only server-sent events as they become available, with the stream terminated by a `data: [DONE]` message' supports option a. No WebSocket, multipart or post-hoc array transport appears in the reference; a is the single best answer.

`temperature` description: 'Higher values like 0.8 will make the output more random, while lower values like 0.2 will make it more focused and deterministic' supports option b. The passage only 'recommends altering this or top_p but not both', so c (auto-disabling top_p) is unsupported; d over-claims byte-identical output; a inverts the source. b is uniquely best.

Rerank page summary 'Reranks documents based on their relevance to a query' and the RerankResult schema (required fields index, document, relevance_score; 'Relevance score of the document') support option c. No vector, rewrite, or completion is returned per the schema; c is uniquely best.

Function-calling Note: 'The model does not execute the functions itself ... You are responsible for parsing these outputs and executing the corresponding functions on your backend or client side', plus the Python example appending {role: tool, content: result, tool_call_id: call.id} after executing, support option d. The 'Execute and Iterate' step contradicts a, b and c. d is uniquely best.

Quickstart Python snippet constructs OpenAI(base_url="https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/v1/", api_key=os.environ.get("NEBIUS_API_KEY")); the JS variant uses the same pair as baseURL/apiKey. Option c is the only pair present in the source; the other three name parameters that do not exist on the client.

Sandboxes overview 'Secure isolation' card: 'VM-level isolation ensures untrusted code cannot escape the sandbox or affect other workloads' directly supports option a. Nothing in the page ties isolation to inference speed, API keys or HTML conversion; a is uniquely best.

'Educational platforms' use-case card: 'Provide students with safe code execution environments. Automatic cleanup and resource limits help prevent abuse' supports option b. Beta limitations state 'Number of simultaneously running operations is limited to 50', which contradicts d; the page describes Git-like branching/checkpoints, not automatic git commits (a); DNS is absent (c). b is uniquely best.

JSON page: 'JSON schema following. Follows the specific schema you provide - {type: json_schema}' vs 'Arbitrary JSON object. Forces arbitrary JSON output, the model will decide on the schema by itself {type: json_object}', and the Tip 'Use JSON schema instead of JSON objects whenever you need strict JSON structure' support option a. b and d contradict the distinction; c ignores the response_format the page prescribes (prompt instruction is described as additional). a is uniquely best.

Datasets page basic conversational example uses roles system, user, assistant; the 'Tool-augmented conversations' example adds {role: tool, tool_call_id: call_1, name: get_weather}. Option a matches exactly. b, c and d name roles/fields absent from the messages examples (query/document are rerank fields). a is uniquely best.

Datasets page opening: 'Nebius Token Factory supports the JSON Lines format (.jsonl) for dataset files', and all four dataset types (conversational, instruction, text, pretokenized) are shown as JSON objects per line. Option d is the only documented format; XML, CSV and protobuf are absent. d is uniquely best.

Fine-tuning walkthrough step 2: 'training_file = client.files.create(file=open("training.jsonl","rb"), purpose="fine-tune")' and 'You only need the id fields from these responses to create a fine-tuning job'; API spec: 'training_file (string, required) ID of the file with the training dataset (purpose = "fine-tune")'. Option a matches; inline rows, purpose=assistants/name reference, and URLs are not documented inputs. a is uniquely best.

Hyperparameters section: 'n_epochs (integer, optional) Number of passes over the entire dataset. Range 1–20. Default 3' supports option c. batch_size and learning_rate are documented with different meanings (learning_rate: 'Step size for gradient descent'); temperature is not a fine-tuning hyperparameter on the page. c is uniquely best.

Hyperparameters section: 'lora_r (integer, optional) Rank of LoRA matrices. Higher values increase capacity but also overfitting and cost' supports option d. lora_dropout ('Dropout applied to LoRA layers'), weight_decay ('L2 regularization factor'), context_length are each documented with a different meaning. d is uniquely best.

Lifecycle page, Readiness Status: 'Partially ready — Endpoint can serve traffic, but below expected capacity. Some replicas are still starting, updating, or unavailable' matches the stem scenario exactly, supporting option d. 'Not ready' = cannot reliably serve; 'Ready' = fully provisioned; 'Warning' is listed under Lifecycle Status, not Readiness. d is uniquely best.

Readiness Status: 'Ready — Endpoint is fully provisioned and ready for expected traffic' supports option a. Key Principle note 'Lifecycle is deployment state. Readiness is traffic-serving capability' and the examples table (Running paired with Partially ready / Not ready) rule out b and d as readiness statuses; c is defined as below expected capacity. a is uniquely best.

Dedicated vs Public comparison row '| Custom weights support | Supported for eligible models | Base models only |' supports option b. Same table gives 'Per GPU/hour' pricing (contradicts c) and 'Deployment region is fixed and user-selected' (contradicts d); capacity page states 'Self-service dedicated endpoints do not include a formal SLA unless covered by contract' (contradicts a). b is uniquely best.

Control & Data Plane terminology table: 'routing_key — The model identifier you pass to inference calls. Returned when you create an endpoint' supports option a; 'endpoint_id — Identifier used for update/delete operations' rules out b; Flavor is defined as a template sub-option (c); the control plane 'has common base URL API' for management, not inference (d). a is uniquely best.

Comparison row '| Pricing | Per GPU/hour, billed with per-minute granularity | Per token |' (dedicated vs public serverless columns) supports option b exactly. No storage, query, licence or per-request basis appears in the source. b is uniquely best.

Rate Limits & Scaling page, 'Monitoring your headroom and handling 429s': 'If you exceed the active limit you will receive HTTP 429' supports option a; the page describes the dynamic limits of the shared inference tier, consistent with the comparison table's 'Dynamic rate limits apply' for public serverless. 500/404/401 are not mentioned as rate-limit responses. a is uniquely best.

Quickstart: 'client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/v1/", ...)' (and baseURL in the JS variant) supports option a. The three distractors are URLs that appear nowhere in the source. a is uniquely best.

Reviewed 2026-09-06 after the option-a explanation edit (commit d3366e1). EVIDENCE CAVEAT: the evidence pins src-inference-overview sha 344d6de4815469a58d7c91b6e7e02043136b35360334480452ea39b79a32eeca; no local snapshot with that hash exists (R2 only; Evidence CI verified the excerpt against it). Context was read from the LIVE revision captured at scratchpad inference-overview-live.md (sha 9f0c64e301e182dae90c19112f4d077c8ff44a54d2e1138be49f8ede18b39340), not from the pinned bytes. In the live page the Quantization card reads exactly "A technique that reduces the precision of model weights and activations, decreasing memory usage and computation", which supports the stem (lower numeric precision of the model to reduce memory) and option d. The sibling cards define KV Cache (stores frequently accessed key-value pairs, reducing computations), Paged Attention (memory-management technique that partitions each request KV cache into fixed-size blocks, stored non-contiguously, reducing fragmentation) and Continuous Batching (batches multiple input sequences together, increasing throughput); none mentions precision, so a, b and c are ruled out and d is uniquely best. The rewritten option-a explanation matches the Paged Attention wording that commit 07a74e8 records for the pinned 344d6de4 revision and that the live page still carries; the other three explanations do not contradict the live definitions. Residual risk: the pinned bytes were not inspected directly; the approval rests on CI verbatim verification of the excerpt plus the commit-recorded pinned wording of the Paged Attention card.

Dataset Formats, section 'Tool-augmented conversations': 'Each training example can optionally include a `tools` field that defines the tools available in that conversation. The schema should match what you plan to use at inference time', followed by a JSON example with a top-level `tools` array and the key point '`tools` is optional'. That supports option b in both halves (optional field on the example; schema matching inference). The page documents JSON Lines files only, no binary payloads, no prompt-comment convention and no webhooks, so a, c and d have no support; b is the single best answer. Option-a explanation ('plain JSON Lines') matches the page's opening statement.

Data Lab Overview, first paragraphs: 'the unified workspace inside Nebius Token Factory for working with inference logs (chat completions) and datasets' plus the three bullets 'view, filter, and export inference logs', 'preparing datasets via SQL queries' and 'Reusable datasets for batch inference and fine-tuning'. Option a restates exactly those three bullets. The page contains nothing about TLS certificates or Kubernetes nodes (b, c), and the SQL queries are described as creating 'Filtered Datasets ... from inference logs', not querying external production databases (d). Option a is the single best answer.

Supervised Fine-Tuning, Python step 2 uploads both training.jsonl and validation.jsonl with purpose="fine-tune"; the cURL tab uses -F 'purpose=fine-tune' and the response echoes "purpose": "fine-tune"; the API specification says training_file is the 'ID of the file with the training dataset (purpose = "fine-tune")', which backs the second clause of the option-b explanation. No other purpose value appears anywhere on the page, so a, c and d (user_avatar, web_search, cache_backup) are unsupported and b is the single best answer.

Supervised Fine-Tuning, Python step 6 'Inspect job events (optional but recommended)': 'Events help you understand the lifecycle (file validation, dataset processing, training progress)' immediately followed by the code 'events = client.fine_tuning.jobs.list_events(job.id)'; the cURL tab exposes the same via GET /v1/fine_tuning/jobs/<job_ID>/events. The stem's three examples are the page's own parenthetical. No serial console (a) or DNS (c) is mentioned, and /v1/models (d) does not appear on the page at all; the only other progress source the page names is the job object itself (trained_steps/total_steps), which is not one of the options. Option b is the single best answer.

Supervised Fine-Tuning, 'Hyperparameters': '`lora` (boolean, optional) Whether to use LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) instead of full-parameter fine-tuning. true: only LoRA adapter weights are trained; base model weights stay frozen. false: full fine-tuning is applied.' Option c is that sentence; a is the documented `lora: false` behaviour (the option-a explanation says so correctly), d inverts the sentence, and nothing on the page singles out the embedding layer (b). Single best answer: c.

Merging LoRA Adapters intro: 'inference usually requires loading both the base model and the LoRA adapter. Here we provide a merge script that bakes the LoRA adapters directly into the base weights and produces a standard checkpoint directory' answers the stem. The rewritten option d ('for each merged layer's weight tensor it adds the scaled product B @ A') now matches the script exactly: _merge_lora_weight computes 'deltaW = B @ A; merged_weight = tensor + scale * deltaW' and _process_single_file applies it only when _needs_lora_merge(tensor_name) and tensor_name.endswith('.weight'), storing every other tensor unchanged. The explanation's default scope is the page's own 'Notes & constraints': 'By default, only layers matching ALLOWED_LORA_LAYERS = [r"model.layers.*.self_attn"] are merged. If you trained LoRA on other modules (e.g. MLPs), extend ALLOWED_LORA_LAYERS accordingly'; 'produces a standard checkpoint directory' and 'copied unchanged' are supported by the intro and by 'All non-.safetensors files are copied from the original checkpoint directory'. Nothing on the page describes gradient accumulation, dataset deduplication or prompt prefixing, so a, b and c have no support and d is the single best answer. Previous rejection (quantifier 'each base tensor') is resolved.

Supervised Fine-Tuning, Prerequisites step 2: 'Optionally, create a validation dataset as well. A typical split is: 80–90% of examples → training, 10–20% of examples → validation'. Option c reproduces that split. 50/50 (a) and 99/1 (b) fall outside the documented range, and d ('equal-sized files are mandatory') is contradicted twice: the validation set is 'Optionally' created and the split is unequal; the option-c explanation's 'validation dataset is optional' is the same sentence. Single best answer: c. Reviewed as a fresh item under a new ID; the earlier q-ds01c3d4e5f6 revision that tested the rationale for splitting has no supporting passage on this page and stays needs_review.

Supervised Fine-Tuning, 'Hyperparameters' section: '`learning_rate` (float, optional) Step size for gradient descent. Must be >= 0. Typical values: 1e-6–5e-5. Default: 0.00001'. Option d matches the definition and range, and every clause of its explanation (>= 0, typical range, default) is on the page. Each distractor is the page's definition of a different hyperparameter (n_epochs 'Number of passes over the entire dataset', range 1–20; lora_r 'Rank of LoRA matrices', range 8–128; warmup_ratio 'Fraction of total training steps used for linear warmup', range 0–1), so none describes learning_rate and d is the single best answer. Reviewed as a fresh item under a new ID; the earlier q-ft04d8e9f0a1 revision about a too-high learning rate has no supporting passage on this page (only max_grad_norm has documented too-high/too-low consequences) and stays needs_review.

Dedicated endpoints overview, Autoscaling card: 'Set minimum and maximum replicas to automatically scale capacity with traffic', and comparison table row 'Autoscaling | You control minimum and maximum replicas'. Capacity page, section 'Maximum replicas scaling': 'Scaling above minimum replicas depends on available burst capacity and is not guaranteed indefinitely. Additional replicas may be reclaimed after scale-down'. Both halves of option a are supported in context. b is contradicted by the user-set maximum and the burst caveat; d is contradicted by autoscaling and by 'Create, update, stop, and delete deployments'; c has no basis, the overview presents dedicated capacity as 'Isolated capacity reserved for your organization' and no fallback to serverless appears anywhere in either page. a is uniquely best.

Overview comparison table row 'Capacity | Isolated capacity reserved for your organization | Shared multi-tenant capacity' supports the core contrast in option a. The qualifier 'while the endpoint runs' is supported by the capacity page: 'allocated to your endpoint only while it is active — it is not a long-term reservation, and the minimum replicas guarantee applies only while the endpoint is running'. b is directly contradicted by that sentence and by 'When an endpoint stops, its GPU capacity is released back to the shared pool. This applies regardless of why the endpoint stopped' (manual stop, incident, maintenance). c and d invert the table row. a is uniquely best.

Rate Limits & Scaling page, section 'Over-the-Limit Processing': 'requests that exceed your rate limit may still be processed. This occurs when the system has spare capacity available, and your request can be handled with a lower priority', the response 'x-ratelimit-over-limit: yes', and 'Treat this as an early warning—subsequent calls may be throttled'; the header table repeats this ('Set to "yes" if a request that is over the limit is processed'). Option a is supported in full. b is contradicted: 'If you exceed the active limit you will receive HTTP 429' is the normal case, but the same page documents the spare-capacity exception, and the stem fixes the spare-capacity condition. c has no basis: the 15-minute buckets adjust the limit (x1.2 / /1.5), nothing describes queuing a request. d has no basis on this page or on the dedicated-endpoints pages. a is uniquely best. Objective move: the question as written tests over-the-limit processing of a request against a dynamic rate limit on public serverless endpoints, which is exactly what this rate-limits page covers; it does not test dedicated-endpoint capacity (burst replicas, GPU pool), which is what domain-4/capacity-and-scaling covers per the capacity page. The concept was always 'what happens to a request beyond the nominal limit when spare capacity exists', and domain-4/rate-limits is the honest home for it; the relabel corrects a mismatch rather than disguising a different concept.

Create chat completion reference, components.schemas.Usage: completion_tokens 'Number of tokens in the generated completion', prompt_tokens 'Number of tokens in the prompt', total_tokens 'Total number of tokens used in the request (prompt + completion)'; ChatCompletionResponse.usage references this schema and is required. The response example shows the same three fields. Option a is supported. The schema also carries prompt_tokens_details and completion_tokens_details (breakdowns, nullable), which the stem does not mention; this makes a slightly under-inclusive but not wrong, and no distractor is affected. b, c, d name hardware, transport and database metrics that appear nowhere in the reference. a is uniquely best.

Organizations and Projects, 'Hierarchy Overview': 'Organization → Projects → Resources'; 'Each Project within an organization acts as an isolated environment for related resources and teams'; 'Resources—such as models, endpoints, files, and datasets—exist inside a project and inherit its access settings'. Option d is supported in full. a is contradicted by 'isolated environment' and by access being granted via groups; b is contradicted by 'within an organization' and by 'Within a project, you can create and manage: API keys'; c is contradicted by 'a default project is created automatically' at sign-up, with no identity provider mentioned on the page. Minor: the d explanation lists API keys among the inheriting resources while the inherit sentence names models, endpoints, files, datasets; API keys are listed as project resources in the next section, so this is not a contradiction. d is uniquely best.

Organizations and Projects, 'Projects' section: 'Each project includes Project Groups that control access to project resources', set against the 'Organization' section: 'To grant a user access to organizational resources, add them to the relevant Organization Group'. The stem asks about access to one project's resources without organization-wide access, which maps to Project Groups; option b is supported. a fails on its own wording ('the only access mechanism') because Project Groups exist and are the documented control for project resources. c has no basis: API keys are listed as resources created within a project, never as a way to grant a user access. d misreads 'Projects can be multi-region, allowing you to group resources by product, team, use case', which is about organising resources, not access. b is uniquely best.

Organizations and Projects, 'Projects' section: 'Within a project, you can create and manage: API keys, Fine-tuning jobs, Dedicated endpoints, Files and datasets'; the hierarchy diagram draws exactly these four under Project A. Option a is supported. d is contradicted by the hierarchy 'Organization → Projects → Resources' and by the organization being described as containing projects, organization groups and user accounts; b has no basis, user accounts appear only as members with groups and permissions; c is contradicted by 'Projects can be multi-region', so regions are not a containing scope. a is uniquely best.

Model Deprecations: August 2026, 'What to Know': 'After that date, you will not be able to select them in the Playground or send API requests using their model IDs' and 'Token Factory does not automatically reroute requests from deprecated models'. Both clauses of option a are supported. b is directly contradicted by the no-reroute bullet. c is contradicted twice: the Note says 'Dedicated Endpoints for these models will be unaffected by this change' and the bullet says 'This change only affects Serverless usage'. d has no basis; the page talks about model IDs and migration, never credentials. Note the stem says 'published deprecation date' generically while the page is about one specific date; the behaviour described is the same. a is uniquely best.

Organizations and Projects, 'Organization' section: 'When you sign up for Nebius Token Factory, a personal organization is created automatically. You can also: Be invited to other organizations and collaborate on their projects; Create additional organizations for separate teams or business units'. Option a restates both bullets. b is contradicted by those bullets; c and d add conditions (per-organization payment card, 24-hour window) that appear nowhere on the page. a is uniquely best.

Quickstart cURL example: -H "Authorization: Bearer $NEBIUS_API_KEY" against https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/v1/chat/completions; the Python and JavaScript examples pass the same NEBIUS_API_KEY as api_key / apiKey, and the 'Get API key' accordion says 'For authentication, get an API key'. The chat completion reference on the same host declares security HTTPBearer. Option a is supported. b, c, d (mTLS certificate, password header, IP allowlist) appear nowhere in the quickstart. Single evidence item, but it is the canonical authenticated request and needs no second source. a is uniquely best.

UI & Playground, 'Model card' section: 'To view an extended list of model parameters via the API, send a request to the List models endpoint with the query parameter verbose=true'. List models reference: OpenAPI path 'get /v1/models' with a query parameter 'verbose' (boolean, default false), and the RichModel schema lists context_length (integer, required). Option a is supported by both sources read together, including the exact path and the example parameter named in the stem. b, c, d are not mechanisms the docs describe. a is uniquely best.

UI & Playground: 'The Playground in Nebius Token Factory lets you experiment with available AI models through a web interface — no coding required', and 'Compare setups': 'To work with two model setups side by side, click Compare. This will open two chat windows where you can submit inputs for both setups at the same time'. Option a is supported in full. b, c, d are unrelated to anything on the page. a is uniquely best.

Create chat completion reference, ChatCompletionRequest.temperature: 'What sampling temperature to use, between 0 and 2. Higher values like 0.8 will make the output more random, while lower values like 0.2 will make it more focused and deterministic'. Option a is supported. The only other sampling parameter with a related description, top_p (nucleus sampling, probability mass), is not offered as an option, so no distractor is defensible; b, c, d are transport, scheduling and display settings that appear nowhere in the reference. a is uniquely best.
